transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Silva (Redwood SRE); Dana Ruiz (Orion - Lead ML Eng), Michael Chen (Orion - Platform Eng), Sara O'Neill (Orion - Product)

Summary: quick check-in on pilot latency numbers, focus on TTFT (time-to-first-token) improvements with streaming on, sequence length distribution impact, and kernel choices. Reviewed recent microbenchmarks, discussed prefix/KV cache behavior and batching windows. Agreed action items and kernel workshop.

Topics: TTFT delta vs baseline, streaming vs chunked responses, quantization trade-offs, kernel selection (attention kernel + matrix multiply path), sequence length realistic profiles, caching hit rates, production rollout plan for dedicated burst.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: ok everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give it about an hour, main things — review the numbers Priya ran, any surprises from the last week, then agree next steps. Dana, hi, how's the week been on your side?
[00:18] Dana: hey alex, thanks. pretty busy, yeah we've been running the feature branch in staging, saw some improvements but TTFT is still spiky on longer prompts, so wanted to dig into that.
[00:35] Priya: sure, i'll start with the numbers — i ran the 3 configs we talked about, baseline (fp16, default kernel), fp16 with streaming enabled and small batching window, and 4-bit quantized with alternative matmul kernel. sample size ~200 per config but weighted to your 95th seq lengths.
[00:54] Priya: baseline TTFT median ~120ms, 95th ~420ms. streaming test gave median ~95ms, 95th ~300ms — so about 25-30% improvement in TTFT for the heavy tails. the 4-bit run reduced token cost but increased variance, 95th moved to ~380ms with occasional spikes.
[01:20] Michael: that variance on 4-bit — is that because of kernel fallback or because the quant path isn't pinned to the same kernels?
[01:29] Priya: yeah good question. it's a mix — the quant runtime will choose different matmul kernels and we saw a few fallback paths hitting int8 emulation on p3 which added overhead. also KV cache alignment on longer sequences caused some cache misses we didn't expect.
[01:45] Marco: to add, we noticed the cache hit rate on that sample set was only ~12% for prefix-level caching because your requests often have slightly different prefixes; when we canonicalize prompts the hit rate moves toward ~38%. so a prompt normalization step could help.
[02:05] Dana: hmm interesting, our front-end does a lot of templating, maybe we can normalize. but we're worried about accidental prompt rewrites changing behavior.
[02:15] Alex: yeah that's a common tradeoff, normalization helps latency but we should define exact rules and a quick A/B on behavior.
[02:25] Priya: also streaming chunk size matter — we tested 16-token chunks vs 4-token chunks. 4-token gave faster TTFT but more overhead per-stream frame; 16-token lowered overhead but slightly increased first payload delay. for the user experience you guys described (progressive text), 8-token seemed like a good compromise.
[02:48] Sara: can you clarify — TTFT here equals time to first byte returned or time until first token parsed by client? which metric are we using?
[02:55] Priya: it's measured as time to first token at the SDK layer — so includes serialization and small network latency. the SDK is about 8-12ms on average, so purely runtime TTFT is slightly lower.
[03:10] Michael: were these runs on the hosted cluster or on our dedicated pilot nodes?
[03:15] Priya: these were on your dedicated pilot nodes (the p4d-style machines we provisioned) — we repeated the most critical ones on hosted to compare and the delta was minimal for median, larger for tails.
[03:27] Alex: ok, let's walk through a couple of concrete cases you flagged last week — the 1.2k token prompt that showed a 1.2s TTFT spike. Priya, what did you see?
[03:36] Priya: for that trace, sequence length pushed KV cache allocation into a different bucket and caused an extra memory copy during the first generation step; that copy is about 400ms on p3 with the older kernel. switching to the newer fused attention kernel removed that copy and brought TTFT down to ~450ms.
[03:52] Marco: that fused kernel has better memory layout for long sequences but it's more sensitive to alignment, so when we enable it we need to ensure the compilation path picks the right tiling. the runtime can pick it automatically but needs a complete kernel matrix run which i'd like to do during our workshop.
[04:12] Dana: what's the risk of compatibility — do we risk different output tokens when switching kernels?
[04:18] Priya: in general no, numeric differences are within usual FP nondeterminism, but quantized kernels can change rounding and occasionally impact rare tokens. we flagged one prompt where 4-bit made the model prefer an alternate token in ~0.7% of generations.
[04:32] Sara: that could be a blocker for us on medical content, we need consistency for a subset of prompts.
[04:38] Alex: understood — so we should define a policy: floating point kernels for the safety-critical prompt set, quant or lower-precision for others. we can set route rules in the pilot to pin model variants per prompt tag.
[04:51] Michael: routing sounds good, how do we tag prompts? can we add metadata in the call?
[04:56] Priya: yes, pass a header or metadata field in the request; we support prompt tags that map to model/profile routes.
[05:05] Alex: ok next, batching window — Marco, you had an experiment where reducing the batching window to 15ms changed P99 for some cases?
[05:12] Marco: right — shrinking the batching window reduces latency for single-user TTFT but can harm throughput and increase cost. for your profile the effective concurrency is low (1.4 avg) so a 20ms window gives best unit cost while keeping TTFT under target. at 5ms median helps but P95 sometimes regresses due to fragmentation.
[05:33] Dana: is the 1.4 concurrency number from our traces? we've seen spikes during morning syncs where concurrency jumps to 8-10.
[05:40] Michael: yeah we have periodic batch jobs hitting the API, that might be causing spikes.
[05:44] Priya: then we should configure autoscale burst capacity for those windows — dedicated burst increases cost slightly but keeps latency SLOs. Alex i'll share a cost delta sheet.
[05:53] Alex: noted, will send that.
[06:00] (--- 10-minute deep dive on kernel matrix choreography ---)
[16:05] Priya: quick note on streaming protocol — we tested gRPC streaming vs HTTP chunked. gRPC had slightly lower overhead on our internal net but your front-end stack is more HTTP friendly. we can emulate the gRPC framing in HTTP streams and still get most benefits.
[16:27] Michael: great, easier for us to adopt. any SDK changes required?
[16:32] Priya: small ones; we'll share a patch for the JS SDK that supports 8-token chunk streaming with backoff.
[16:40] Dana: you mentioned earlier a prompt-normalization approach — can you give examples? I worry about changing patient identifiers etc.
[16:47] Marco: normalization we propose is structural: remove variable whitespace, canonicalize certain template placeholders to a token, but do not rewrite user-provided data. so IDs remain identical. basically normalize the template layer not the payload.
[17:03] Dana: ok that sounds safer. we'll try a small pass in staging and measure cache hit change.
[17:10] Priya: on the kernel side, recommended immediate next step — run the kernel-selection matrix across your pilot hardware with your real prompt distribution. that gives us a deterministic pick for fused-attention vs default.
[17:22] Sara: what about the 4-bit quant plan — any further mitigations for the occasional token drift?
[17:28] Priya: yes, we can scope 4-bit to a subset of endpoints where we don't have safety constraints; also run A/B evals on a held-out prompt set to quantify behavioral deltas. if the delta exceeds threshold we keep fp16 for that route.
[17:42] Alex: good. let's talk about measurement — we need to standardize metrics across teams. Priya, can you propose a template?
[17:48] Priya: sure — we'll output median/95/99 TTFT, median/95 token latency, KV cache hit rate, frames-per-response (stream chunks), and cost per 1k tokens. will share a google sheet link (drive.redwood/pilot-orion-ttft).
[18:02] Michael: please include trace IDs for the 10 outlier requests. that will help root cause.
[18:06] Priya: yep will do.
[18:10] (brief crosstalk)
[18:20] Dana: one thing — in earlier runs you saw ~400ms memory-copy overhead; is that something we can fix without kernel change? like different memory allocator?
[18:28] Marco: possibly — tuning the allocator and preallocating larger KV buffers reduces copies. we can try an allocator tweak in the runtime config for the pilot. low risk.
[18:37] Alex: good candidate for quick win. Priya can you schedule that with Marco?
[18:41] Priya: yes i'll do that today.
[18:45] Sara: also curious about fallback behavior — if we hit capacity or a kernel fails do we have graceful fallback to smaller model or hosted path?
[18:53] Alex: yes, we can configure routing policies: fallback to a smaller model family with preserved prompt mapping, or route to hosted with slightly higher latency but guaranteed availability. we'll capture defaults in the runbook.
[19:05] Michael: can we set different SLAs by route? like strict for critical prompts, best-effort for exploratory ones?
[19:11] Alex: yep, route-level SLOs are supported. we'll include recommended SLAs for pilot vs prod.
[19:18] Priya: quick note on instrumentation — add token-level debug traces for the first 100 responses so we can see where the pipeline stalls. enable at sample rate 1% in staging.
[19:28] Dana: ok good.
[19:35] (--- sample logs and a small benchmark review: 20:00–34:00) ---
[34:02] Priya: ran one more test: canonicalized prompts + 8-token streaming + fused kernel gave median TTFT of 80ms and 95th of 210ms on your pilot — that's a big improvement. cost delta was +6% vs baseline due to slightly higher compute per token but we cut user-perceived latency a lot.
[34:24] Sara: sounds promising, would prefer lower P95 even if cost climbs a little.
[34:30] Michael: can you also quantify added tail variance when concurrency spikes to 8?
[34:36] Marco: with the canonicalized config and 20ms batching window at concurrency 8, P95 stayed ~260ms, P99 around 420ms. acceptable given our SLA goals but we'll need burst capacity for the peak windows.
[34:52] Alex: so tradeoff summary: canonicalization + fused kernel + 8-token streaming + 20ms batching gives best user latency; 4-bit helps cost but increases behavioral delta and variance; allocator + kernel workshop could shave another 100–150ms off bad traces.
[35:10] Dana: agreed. let's plan the kernel workshop and i'll share the 50 traces.
[35:16] Alex: action items recap — Priya runs kernel matrix; Dana shares traces; Alex sends pricing. Marco will try allocator tweak and we will reconvene next week.
[35:29] Michael: one more question on security — we need SOC2 docs for the dedicated nodes, can you send updated attestation?
[35:36] Alex: yes, i'll attach SOC2 + ISO docs and our runbook for audit.
[35:41] (--- wrap up and scheduling: 35:41–54:00) ---
[44:02] Priya: scheduling note — propose kernel workshop next Tuesday 2025-11-11 at 16:00 UTC, 90 minutes. will invite runtime engineers.
[44:10] Dana: works for us, put Michael and me.
[44:14] Alex: i'll create calendar invite and include agenda.
[44:20] Sara: thanks all, appreciate the concrete wins.
[44:25] Alex: thanks team, see you next week.

End of transcript.

Recap (quick):
- Immediate wins: prompt canonicalization trial, allocator tweak, 8-token streaming default for pilot.
- Medium: run kernel matrix on pilot hardware, pin fused kernel for long-seq routes.
- Long: evaluate selective 4-bit quantization after A/B checks and safety gating.

Links referenced: drive.redwood/pilot-orion-ttft (benchmark sheet), drive.redwood/kernel-matrix, redwood.com/security/soc2.pdf

Next meeting: weekly POC sync — 2025-11-11 (kernel workshop scheduled)
